panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of an infant's genital/perineal (diaper) area with a real, untreated napkin rash, matching the configured target disease diaper_dermatitis. The caption and in-text explicitly identify an extensive, inflamed, damaged napkin rash, supporting confluent diaper-area erythema with probable superficial erosion. No diagram, control, other disease, or third-party issue is present; prior triage also routed this figure to keep.
panels.attribution_text: Alkhuder and Mawlawi. Infantile Iatrogenic Cushing Syndrome due to Topical Steroids.. Case reports in pediatrics 2019. doi:10.1155/2019/2652961. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: The patient's genitalia showing the napkin rash.
in_text_mentions: The patient's physical examination revealed facial puffiness (Figure 1) and generalized body edema (Figure 2). There were no abdominal stria, and the cutaneous examination revealed nothing but the napkin rash (Figure 3). The infant was vitally stable with no dysmorphic features and no skeletal deformities. Her growth parameters were within normal limits, and her systemic examination was unremarkable.

In our case, clobetasol is not the topical steroid of choice for the management of the napkin rash. As shown in Figure 3, the rash is extensive, and the skin was inflamed and damaged. This allows more permeation and penetration of the topical medication. Thus, it was better to choose a low potency topical steroid, e.g., hydrocortisone than to choose a very potent agent such as clobetasol [17]. Furthermore, screening methods such as midnight salivary cortisol could prove to be helpful in early detection of potential iatrogenic Cushing syndrome while using topical steroids [18]. panels.rationale: The article title explicitly frames granuloma gluteale infantum as a complication of diaper dermatitis, and the figure shows the initial clinical presentation with multiple purple-red indurated nodules on the gluteal area in an infant. The image is a real patient photograph clearly depicting lesions in diaper distribution. The erythema in the diaper area is tagged from the vocabulary; the defining nodular lesions of GGI are not represented in the allowed vocabulary and are placed in proposed_findings. Typicality is atypical because GGI is a rare, forgotten complication with a nodular presentation that is not the common clinical picture of diaper dermatitis. [raw subtype: granuloma_gluteale_infantum]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of the diaper/genital distribution with marked erythema and scaling, directly matching diaper dermatitis vocabulary findings. B: Real patient photograph captioned as part of the initial presentation of diaper dermatitis; the disease-focused article title specifies disseminated diaper dermatitis with concomitant body rash, supporting attribution of this maculopapular body rash though it is not represented in the allowed findings vocabulary. C: Clinical photograph of the same patient showing the captioned trunk maculopapular rash on day 3; attribution to diaper dermatitis comes from the disease-focused case title describing disseminated diaper dermatitis with concomitant body rash, with moderate confidence because the body-rash finding is outside the allowed diaper-area vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Initial presentation of diaper dermatitis (A) Genital area showing marked erythema, flaking, and scaling. (B) Maculopapular rash involving the face, hands, and chest, appearing on the third day. (C) Maculopapular rash on the trunk was also noted on the third day.
in_text_mentions: A six-month-old male with a history of redundant prepuce and phimosis presented to the office with a diaper rash that had begun five days earlier. The patient had experienced a similar-appearing diaper rash one month prior, which had resolved spontaneously without medical intervention. There were no preceding lesions, such as a herald patch, before the onset of the current diaper rash. According to the patient’s mother, a body rash developed on day 3 of the illness. An erythematous maculopapular rash was observed on the abdomen, chest, cheeks, arms, and hands (Figure 1).
